prompt: You add a column to the `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS book` statement in `schema.sql` and restart against the database the application has been using. What happens to the `book` table?
hint: Read what `IF NOT EXISTS` checks for.

choices.text: It gains the new column on that start
choices.why: That is the picture of `schema.sql` as a description of the schema. It describes an empty database only; an existing table is left as it is.

choices.text: Nothing changes: the whole statement is skipped
choices.why: `IF NOT EXISTS` finds a table called `book` and skips the statement, new column included, without an error or a log line.

choices.text: The start fails because `book` already exists
choices.why: That is what would happen without the guard. The guard exists precisely so that the second start does not fail.

choices.text: Spring Boot drops the table and creates it again with the column
choices.why: Spring Boot's script runner never drops anything on its own. Dropping and recreating is Hibernate's `create`, a different setting.

prompt: Why did lesson 10's `data.sql` end each `INSERT` with `ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING`?
hint: When did that file run?

choices.text: To skip any row whose price breaks the `CHECK` constraint
choices.why: `ON CONFLICT` handles unique and primary key conflicts, not a failed `CHECK`; a negative price would still stop the insert.

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL requires it on an insert of several rows
choices.why: A multi-row `INSERT` works without it, as `V2__first_titles.sql` shows.

choices.text: Because the file ran on every start, and the second insert of the same names would fail on their unique constraints
choices.why: Every statement in a file that runs at each start has to be harmless the second time. A migration runs once, so V2 drops the guard.

choices.text: To make the inserts faster when the table is large
choices.why: It changes what happens on a conflict, not how fast anything runs.

prompt: With `spring.sql.init.mode=always`, which of these can `schema.sql` NOT do for a database that already exists? Choose all that apply.
hint: The file has no memory and runs whole each time.

choices.text: Change a column of an existing table, without a guard written by hand for that change
choices.why: An `ALTER` works once and fails on every later start, so each change would need its own guard, forever.

choices.text: Create a table that does not exist yet
choices.why: This it can do: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` creates the missing table and skips the ones that exist.

choices.text: Say which version of the file this database last received
choices.why: Nothing records which version ran, which is exactly what `flyway_schema_history` adds.

choices.text: Bring a database created months ago to the same schema as one created today
choices.why: Each copy started from a different version of the file, and the guards stop the old one from ever catching up.

prompt: What version and description does Flyway read from the file name `V2__first_titles.sql`?
hint: Two underscores separate the two halves.

choices.text: Version 2, description `first titles`
choices.why: The part between `V` and the double underscore is the version; the rest, underscores turned into spaces, is the description.

choices.text: Version `2__first`, description `titles`
choices.why: That would split at the last underscore. The separator is the double underscore, which comes first.

choices.text: Version 2, description `V2__first_titles`
choices.why: The description is what follows the separator, without the version in front of it.

choices.text: Version 1, because it is the second file in the directory
choices.why: Flyway takes the version from the name, never from the file's position in a listing.

prompt: `db/migration` holds `V1__a.sql`, `V2__b.sql`, `V10__c.sql` and `V9__d.sql`. Put them in the order Flyway applies them to an empty database.
hint: Versions compare as numbers.
trap: Sorted as text, V10 lands right after V1; Flyway compares the versions as numbers, so 10 comes after 9.

prompt: Flyway refuses to start: `Found non-empty schema(s) "public" but no schema history table`. The database is production, with three years of orders, and its tables are exactly what V1 to V4 create. What do you do?
hint: Which way out keeps the data, and which number is the truth?

choices.text: Drop the database and recreate it, so that Flyway can apply V1 to V4 from the start
choices.why: That works on test data. Here it deletes three years of orders.

choices.text: Start it once with `baseline-on-migrate` and `baseline-version=4`
choices.why: The baseline records that the database already holds versions up to 4, and Flyway applies only what comes after.

choices.text: Baseline at version 1, so that V2 to V4 run and confirm the tables
choices.why: V2 to V4 would try to create tables and rows that are already there, and fail or duplicate them.

choices.text: Add `spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrate=true` to `application.properties` for good
choices.why: It would work today, and later it would silently baseline any non-empty database the application is pointed at, the wrong one included.

prompt: Somebody baselined a database at version 2, but it only ever had what V1 creates; V2 is the migration that inserts the first six books. What happens from then on?
hint: What can each check see? V2 adds rows, not columns.

choices.text: Flyway finds V2's checksum missing from the baseline row and refuses to start
choices.why: A baseline row carries no checksum to compare; Flyway takes the claim as given.

choices.text: Flyway applies V2 anyway, because the baseline only covers the schema and not the data
choices.why: A baseline covers every version up to its number, schema or data. V2 is treated as applied.

choices.text: Hibernate's `validate` notices the missing books at start-up
choices.why: `validate` compares tables and column types with the entities. It does not count rows.

choices.text: V2 never runs there, and no check reports it
choices.why: The baseline version is a claim nobody verifies, and missing rows break no rule that Flyway or Hibernate checks.

prompt: Which `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` value makes Hibernate compare the entities with the schema and refuse to start on a difference, changing nothing?
hint: One value only reads.

choices.text: `update`
choices.why: `update` changes the schema towards the entities, which is a second author of the schema beside the migrations.

choices.text: `none`
choices.why: `none` neither changes nor compares: it is how the isbn mismatch went unnoticed in lessons 10 and 11.

choices.text: `create-drop`
choices.why: `create-drop` builds the schema from the entities at start and drops it at shutdown.

choices.text: `validate`
choices.why: It checks and changes nothing, which is the right job for Hibernate once migrations own the schema.

prompt: Why is `ddl-auto=update` the wrong choice in a project that uses Flyway?
hint: Count who writes the schema, and what each one records.

choices.text: It makes start-up slower than `validate` on large schemas
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; both read the whole schema at start.

choices.text: It becomes a second author of the schema, records nothing, and never drops, renames or retypes a column
choices.why: The schema would then be whatever the last entity to start asked for, and no history would say so.

choices.text: Flyway refuses to start whenever `update` is set
choices.why: Flyway does not read Hibernate's settings; the two would run, one after the other.

choices.text: It deletes the rows of every table whose entity changed
choices.why: That describes `create`, which rebuilds the schema. `update` only adds.

prompt: Hibernate says: `wrong column type encountered in column [isbn] in table [book]; found [bpchar (Types#CHAR)], but expecting [varchar(255) (Types#VARCHAR)]`. Which side is which?
hint: `found` is what Hibernate read from the database.

choices.text: The column is `char(n)`; the entity's `String` field, with nothing else said, expects `varchar(255)`
choices.why: `bpchar` is PostgreSQL's name for `char(n)`, and `varchar(255)` is Hibernate's default for a `String`.

choices.text: The column is `varchar(255)`; the entity declares `char`
choices.why: That reads the message backwards: `found` is the database and `expecting` is the entity.

choices.text: The `isbn` column is missing and Hibernate is describing the one it would create
choices.why: A missing column has a message of its own; this one found the column and disliked its type.

choices.text: PostgreSQL has no `varchar`, so Hibernate falls back to `bpchar`
choices.why: PostgreSQL has `varchar`. The two names come from the two sides being compared.

prompt: A migration created `book.isbn` without its `UNIQUE` constraint. `ddl-auto=validate` is set. What happens?
hint: List what `validate` compares.

choices.text: The start fails, because the entity and the table disagree about uniqueness
choices.why: `validate` does not compare constraints, so there is no disagreement for it to find.

choices.text: Hibernate adds the constraint, since `validate` repairs small differences
choices.why: `validate` never changes the schema; repairing is not among its jobs.

choices.text: It starts, and a second book with the same ISBN is accepted
choices.why: `validate` checks tables, columns and types, not `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` or foreign keys. Constraints are the migrations' job.

choices.text: Flyway refuses to start because the table does not match V1's checksum
choices.why: The checksum is computed from the file, not from the table; a file that ran as written matches its row.

prompt: What does the `checksum` column of `flyway_schema_history` let Flyway notice?
hint: It is computed from a file.

choices.text: That somebody changed a table's rows by hand
choices.why: The checksum is computed from the migration file, so nothing done to the data changes it.

choices.text: That a migration file changed after it ran
choices.why: Flyway compares the number stored when the file ran with the number of the file it finds now.

choices.text: That two copies of the application started at the same moment
choices.why: Concurrent starts are a question of locking, not of checksums.

choices.text: That a migration took longer than it did last time
choices.why: Durations go in `execution_time`; the checksum describes the contents.

prompt: A colleague corrects a price inside `V2__first_titles.sql`, which production ran months ago, and deploys. What does production do on its next start?
hint: Compare the file with its row.

choices.text: It applies the new V2, so production gets the corrected price
choices.why: Version 2 has a row already, so Flyway never runs V2 again; it compares it.

choices.text: It starts normally, because only data changed and not the schema
choices.why: The checksum covers the whole file, data or schema. Any edit changes it.

choices.text: It refuses to start with a checksum mismatch and applies nothing
choices.why: The file no longer matches the row that recorded it, and Flyway stops before two databases can quietly disagree.

choices.text: It runs V2 again from the top, inserting the six books a second time
choices.why: Flyway applies a version once. What it does with a changed one is refuse.

prompt: A price in V2 is wrong. Which of these deal with it correctly? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where has V2 run, and what does each action leave in the database?

choices.text: Revert V2 to what ran, and write the correction as the next migration, an `UPDATE`
choices.why: Every database then receives the same steps in the same order, and the history says what happened.

choices.text: Edit V2 and run `repair`, so that the history matches the file
choices.why: `repair` rewrites the stored checksum and runs nothing: the database keeps the old price while the file shows the new one.

choices.text: If V2 has only ever run on your own machine, edit it and recreate your own database
choices.why: Nobody else has seen the old version, so there is no history to keep yet.

choices.text: Edit V2 and delete its row from the history, so that it runs again
choices.why: V2 would insert its six books a second time, against unique constraints that already hold them.

prompt: After `V3__publisher.sql` failed on its second statement, why was there no `publisher` table?
hint: Which database was it, and what can it do with DDL?

choices.text: Flyway ran an undo migration that dropped what V3 had created
choices.why: Flyway's free edition has no undo, and none was written.

choices.text: Flyway checks every statement against the database before running any of them, so the `CREATE TABLE` never ran
choices.why: It ran; the error came from the database on the second statement, line 6.

choices.text: PostgreSQL runs DDL in transactions, and Flyway ran V3 in one, so the failure rolled back the whole file
choices.why: "Changes successfully rolled back": the database was left exactly at version 2.

choices.text: Hibernate's `validate` dropped the table because no entity maps it
choices.why: `validate` changes nothing, and it never ran: the start stopped at Flyway.

prompt: The same `V3__publisher.sql` passes in a test run that starts from an empty database. Why does that prove little about production?
hint: What does the failing statement need in order to fail?

choices.text: Tests use another PostgreSQL version, which accepts that statement
choices.why: The version is not the point; PostgreSQL 16 accepts it too on an empty table.

choices.text: A `NOT NULL` column with no default fails only on a table that has rows, and an empty database has none
choices.why: Every existing row would break the rule; with no rows there is nothing to break. Test against data shaped like production's.

choices.text: Tests run migrations outside transactions, which hides errors
choices.why: Flyway runs them in transactions there too; the statement simply succeeds on an empty table.

choices.text: Test runs skip migrations that add foreign keys
choices.why: Nothing skips them; the reference to `publisher` is valid on an empty table.

prompt: Every book must get a required `publisher_id`, on a shop that is running. Put the steps of expand and contract in order.
hint: Nothing may be required before every row can satisfy it.
items: A migration adds `publisher_id` as a column that may be empty
A release writes `publisher_id` for every new book
A migration fills `publisher_id` for the old rows
trap: Making the column required before the old rows are filled is the V3 that failed in this section.

prompt: On PostgreSQL a failed migration leaves no row behind. On ___, which commits each `CREATE` and `ALTER` the moment it runs, it leaves half the change and a failed row in the history.
hint: The other widely used open-source database the section names.

prompt: What identifies a changeset in Liquibase?
hint: Look at the history table's first three columns.

choices.text: A version number in the changelog's file name
choices.why: That is Flyway's identity. A Liquibase changelog holds many changesets in one file.

choices.text: Its `id`, its `author` and the file it is in, together
choices.why: `databasechangelog` records all three, and the same `id` by another author is another changeset.

choices.text: Its `md5sum`
choices.why: The checksum detects an edit to a changeset; it is not its name.

choices.text: Its position in the changelog
choices.why: Position decides the order of execution, recorded in `orderexecuted`, not the identity.

prompt: Match each Flyway piece with its Liquibase counterpart.
hint: The comparison table at the end of the section.

prompt: A Liquibase changeset dropped the column `notes`, and its written rollback adds `notes` back. After the rollback, what is in the column?
hint: What does a rollback run, and in which direction?

choices.text: The old values, restored from a copy Liquibase kept before the drop
choices.why: Liquibase keeps no copy of data. A rollback is new changes run forward.

choices.text: Nothing: the column is back, empty
choices.why: The rollback re-creates the column; the data went with the drop and no step brings it back.

choices.text: The values stored in `databasechangelog` when the changeset ran
choices.why: That table records which changesets ran, never the rows they touched.

choices.text: The rollback refuses, because a dropped column can never be added back
choices.why: With a written `rollback`, Liquibase runs it; it refuses only when it has neither a written rollback nor one it can generate.

prompt: On two branches, you and a colleague each add a `V4__...sql` with a different description, and both branches are merged. What does Flyway do at the next start?
hint: What identifies a migration in Flyway?

choices.text: It applies both, in the alphabetical order of their descriptions
choices.why: The version is the identity; two files cannot share one, whatever their descriptions.

choices.text: It applies the newer file and ignores the older one
choices.why: Flyway does not look at file dates, and it does not choose silently between two claims.

choices.text: It refuses to start, because two migrations claim version 4
choices.why: Two files with one version are a conflict Flyway will not settle for you: one of them has to become V5.

choices.text: It applies whichever it finds first and records the other as already applied
choices.why: Recording a migration that never ran would be the silent drift Flyway exists to prevent.

prompt: The shop renames `book.title` to `name`, and during a deployment old and new copies of the application run against one database. Which steps belong to a safe sequence? Choose all that apply.
hint: During the deployment, which column does each copy of the application read?

choices.text: A migration adds `name` and copies `title` into it
choices.why: The expand step: both columns exist, so both versions of the code find the one they read.

choices.text: One migration runs `ALTER TABLE book RENAME COLUMN title TO name` with the release
choices.why: The old copies still running would ask for `title` and fail until the deployment ends.

choices.text: The code moves to reading and writing `name`
choices.why: Once every running copy uses `name`, `title` has no readers left.

choices.text: A later migration drops `title`, in a release after nothing reads it
choices.why: The contract step, last, when it can break nobody.

prompt: A database was baselined at version 2, as this lesson showed, and has since received V3 and nothing else. How many rows does its `flyway_schema_history` hold?
hint: V1 and V2 never ran there.
